Boggart is a name used for varied uncanny beings in northern English folklore. Stories attach them to houses, lanes or particular landscape features, with appearances and behavior changing by locality. There is no single universal form. Our troublesome little festival resident draws on regional folklore rather than a modern fantasy franchise.

Boitata is a fiery being in Brazilian folklore, often imagined as a luminous serpent and associated in many retellings with protecting fields or forests. Its name and stories have Indigenous roots, with regional variations. Our glowing festival character is not a dead person; its original ending concerns a landscape cared for.

Brownies are household beings in Scottish folklore, associated with work performed while people sleep. Stories describe complex expectations around appreciation and gifts, and a household can lose its helper through offense. Our festival story is a new, gentle episode about noticing unseen labor, not instructions for performing a traditional offering.

Divs are powerful beings in Persian epic and folktale, including the Shahnameh. They can appear as adversaries, sorcerers or, in some narratives, helpers and builders. Dokkaebi are powerful, unpredictable beings in Korean folklore. Some traditions connect them with old objects, and stories feature wrestling, tricks, songs or unexpected generosity. Duwende are small supernatural beings in Philippine stories and everyday folk beliefs, sometimes associated with homes, earth or particular places. Kalanoro are nature spirits in Malagasy traditions. Ethnographic accounts from northern Madagascar describe small, long-haired beings and their relationships with certain specialists and local places. These are living, varied traditions, not a single island-wide fairy story. Our leaf satchel and garden adventure are an original gentle interpretation.

Kappa are river beings in Japanese folklore, often shown with a shell and a water-filled hollow on the head. Tales may describe mischief, wrestling or dangerous encounters near water. They are not automatically human ghosts. Our version keeps the river setting while giving one kappa an original, friendly task.

Kapre are giant figures associated with large trees in Philippine folklore. Many accounts include smoke or tobacco, features omitted from this family-friendly design. Their imposing scale is part of the storytelling; skin color is not treated as a source of fear. Our festival visitor receives an original wish about company.

Karakoncolos belongs to winter folklore in Türkiye and neighboring regions, with local names and descriptions. Turkish cultural records describe shaggy figures, bells and sticks among its varied features. Our little visitor keeps that wintry silhouette while replacing frightening encounters with an original story about a gentle bell.

Kasa-obake, also called karakasa-obake, is an umbrella-shaped yokai often drawn with one eye, a long tongue and a single leg. Such images turn an everyday object into something delightfully strange. There is no single biography shared by every version. Our umbrella has its own invented rainy-night wish.

Kelpies are shape-shifting water beings in Scottish folklore, commonly taking a horse-like form. Traditional stories warn of dangerous encounters around rivers and lochs. They are not ordinary horses or automatically human ghosts. Our friendly festival episode is an original alternative that retains the water setting while emphasizing a safe crossing.

Krahang appears in Thai folklore as a flying supernatural being associated with household rice-processing tools, especially sieves used as wings. Historical accounts include transformation and possession themes; it is not simply a dead person with wings. Our friendly flyer uses that distinctive equipment in a clearly original festival story.
Krahang checked the ties on his rice-sieve wings while other guests left in cheerful groups. He knew every gust above the village, but the journey always sounded very quiet once the music faded.

Krasue hovered where the lantern light thinned into mist. Through the windows, she could see visitors sharing sweets. Whenever a curtain moved, she drifted farther away before anyone had the chance to speak.

Krasue is a well-known figure in Thai ghost traditions, described with a floating head and frightening bodily features. Those features are softened into light and mist in our artwork. This is an adaptation, not a claim about the original appearance. The gentle festival personality and story are newly imagined.

La Mulata de Cordoba is a legendary woman associated with accusations, confinement and escape on a boat she draws. The name belongs to the historical story, whose versions reflect racial and social prejudice. She is not necessarily a ghost. Our original continuation follows freedom and self-determination without repeating the accusations as truth.

La Pascualita is the subject of a modern local legend in Chihuahua about an unusually lifelike bridal-shop mannequin. Stories say it changes expression or moves; sensational claims about its material are unverified. Our independent design treats it as a legendary animated mannequin, with a new festival story rather than a factual biography.

La Pascualita watched guests pass the shop window on their way to the parade. The reflections made the street look almost close enough to touch, while her display remained perfectly still and carefully arranged.

La Planchada is a nurse figure in Mexican hospital legends, often recognized by a neatly pressed uniform. Different accounts give her different histories and encounters. These are stories, not evidence of supernatural medical care. Our fictional festival episode imagines a thank-you for a caregiver without identifying an actual nurse or patient.
La Planchada straightened a folded cloth at the quiet end of the festival. Nearby lay a box of thank-you cards that had never reached their recipients, each one carefully written and then forgotten.

The Headless Horseman in Washington Irving's The Legend of Sleepy Hollow belongs to a literary tale shaped by local storytelling. Later art and films add their own details. Our independently designed pumpkin-lit rider evokes the Halloween image without copying a screen version, and its peaceful ending is an original festival invention.

The Jersey Devil is a creature of New Jersey's Pine Barrens folklore, described through changing accounts and reported encounters. Wings, hooves and an unusual head appear in familiar depictions. Its stories are legend rather than verified natural history. Our festival visitor is a new, gentle character inspired by that regional tradition.

The Painted Skin is a dark tale in Liaozhai Zhiyi about a dangerous being hiding behind a painted human appearance. Its theme concerns deception, not merely shyness about looks. Our non-graphic festival character keeps the painting motif while giving this separate, original story a chance to practice honesty.
The albasty listened beside the stream, where a knot of reeds had fallen silent. Even the evening breeze could not coax a song from them.
The bake-danuki arrived as a teapot, a lantern and finally an unusually round pumpkin. Everyone admired the costumes, but nobody knew who to invite when the parade stopped for supper.
The banshee began a low song beyond the lanterns. Guests heard the sorrow in it and hurried away. She was left holding the final note, with nobody to hear what followed.

The banshee, or bean si, is an otherworldly female figure whose lament can foretell a death in Irish tradition. She is not normally the killer in these stories. Accounts vary in appearance and association with families. Our original festival tale focuses on listening to grief, rather than treating it as something shameful.

The boggart rattled the cupboard whenever someone reached for a cup. Guests called it another prank, but inside the cramped space sat a carefully folded blanket that kept getting covered in festival supplies.
The brownie had swept the hall, straightened the chairs and polished every lantern before the first guest arrived. Everyone admired the welcoming room. Nobody wondered who had made it that way.
The div built a splendid doorway, then noticed the doorstep was much too tall. The smallest friend could see the welcome light but could not reach it.

The dokkaebi had arranged ribbons for a wrestling contest, then scared away every possible opponent with an overenthusiastic entrance. Alone beneath the banners, it practiced a victory bow that nobody could see.

The dullahan is a headless rider in Irish folklore, traditionally associated with death and frightening nighttime journeys. It is a distinct figure, not another name for the American Sleepy Hollow horseman. Our festival silhouette removes graphic details, while its gentler journey is openly presented as an original imaginative departure.
The dullahan rode through every lantern arch without stopping. The horse knew the rhythm of the road so well that even a quiet patch of grass felt like an unfamiliar kind of place.
The finished lantern shone against the copper fingers. Zheztyrnak held it gently, ready to join the other lights along the mountain path.
The flower opened as the first friend arrived. The pari smiled behind the bright petals; some welcomes simply needed a little more time.

The ghul belongs to Arabic supernatural storytelling and is often associated with deserted places, danger and changing shape. Later literary and popular versions differ, and the English word ghoul does not capture every earlier meaning. This hooded, lantern-bearing visitor is an original gentle design rather than a traditional fixed appearance.

The gumiho is the nine-tailed fox of Korean stories, often able to appear human. Different tellings range from frightening encounters to questions about transformation and belonging. It has its own Korean narrative traditions, despite related fox figures elsewhere in East Asia. Our welcoming festival episode is an original adaptation.

The gumiho stood beyond the festival lights, carefully folding nine tails behind a stone wall. The laughter inside sounded inviting, but she wondered how long a welcome would last if anyone noticed them.

The hidebehind belongs to the exaggerated creatures of North American lumber-camp storytelling. Its defining trick is slipping behind trees or other cover before anyone can get a clear look. The tales can be frightening, but they are folklore, not wildlife reports. Our shy festival version receives an original, friendly invitation.

The hidebehind stayed half hidden, listening while the others traded stories. That was enough for tonight. Friendship had arrived without demanding a grand entrance or a clear view of every mysterious detail.
The ifrit could make a grand burst of light, but the little lantern needed a steady glow. Each excited flicker made its flame wobble.
The jackalope had told so many enormous stories that it could barely remember which mountain it claimed to have jumped. Now the other guests wanted another adventure, and it felt unexpectedly tired.

The jackalope is an antlered rabbit of American tall tales and novelty traditions, strongly associated with the western United States. It is a humorous invented animal, not a confirmed species or a human ghost. Our festival story celebrates that playful storytelling while keeping imagination separate from claims about real wildlife.
The kalanoro carried one seed in a leaf satchel. Every clearing seemed too windy, and every hollow too dark for the small green life inside.
The kappa waited beside an empty picnic spot with a cucumber cut into careful little stars. Since the old footbridge closed, nobody had stopped there long enough to share a snack.
The karakoncolos came down the snowy path with bells ringing everywhere. Even the sleepy lantern keeper jumped at the sound.
The kelpie stood beside an old crossing and watched travelers choose a much longer road. Moonlight shone on its mane, but no one trusted the path that ran close to the dark water.

The marid arrived in a wonderful whirl, and the little bead rolled straight out of reach. Such a small treasure was surprisingly difficult to carry.
The merrow loved the music on shore, but her sea-cap had slipped beneath a festival bench. As the tide changed, the sound of home seemed to move farther away with every wave.

The nasnas appears in Arabic marvel literature and later accounts of Arabian tales. A familiar description gives it one arm and one leg, with a remarkably agile hop. Versions and uses of the name differ. Our rounded, one-eyed felt creature is a non-graphic fantasy interpretation, not a comparison with human bodies or disability.
The nasnas hopped toward the music, but every tune seemed to hurry past. The little scarf bobbed while one foot tried to keep the beat.
The next breeze carried a soft tune across the stream. The albasty rested beside the reeds, long hair stirring gently with the music.

The old lantern had spent years in a storeroom, listening to new electric lights click on outside. Its paper creaked whenever the parade passed, hoping someone might remember the warm light it carried.

The one-eyed giant, Zhalgyz kozdi dau, appears in Kazakh fairy-tale scholarship and collections. Such giants belong to narratives of encounters, danger and ingenuity, rather than to a documented animal species. This miniature woolly visitor has one central eye and a small stone prop; its helpful search is an original festival story.

The painted boat carried her toward that imagined harbor. On arrival, she opened the workshop window and let the sea air in. The next chapter would begin with her choices, rather than someone else's fear.
The pari had brought a flower for the festival, but its petals stayed folded. Around it, every lantern was already shining.
The picture went up at the gate with the painter's own name beneath it. Nobody needed another disguise. The shapeshifter put down the mask and stayed to paint portraits for the other guests.

The puca is a shape-shifting being in Irish folklore, sometimes appearing as a horse or another animal. Tales connect it with unpredictable encounters, mischief and the autumn season. It is not simply the ghost of a dead person. Our festival puca has an original wish about finding a welcome after the tricks.
The puca turned a fence shadow into a dancing horse, then waited for the laughter to fade. Everyone enjoyed the surprise. Yet nobody thought to ask whether the trickster wanted to stay afterward.

The traveler unfolded a paper address so often that its ink had nearly vanished. Every crossroads offered another road, but none sounded like the voice that once called from the doorway at home.

The umbrella practiced a magnificent hop beside the festival gate. But everyone had checked the clear forecast, and nobody needed shelter. It wondered whether a useful life could end simply because the weather changed.
